newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF nominee Guillen has dovish reputation on rates.
newsitem.headline: BoF nominee Guillen has dovish reputation on rates.

text.p: Pierre Guillen, named on Friday to the Bank of France's policy committee, is a former industrialist who has argued in the past for faster interest rate cuts.
Guillen, 69, one of two people named to the monetary policy council to replace outgoing members Jean Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde, was supported for the post by President Jacques Chirac.
Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard, the other new nominee, were both expected to be more open to cutting French interest rates faster than the Bank of France's cautious policy would allow.

Newspapers described Guillen as against monetary union and the "franc fort", a charge that dates from the early 1990s when France had to jack up interest rates to stop currency attacks after German reunification led the Bundesbank to raise rates.
An outsider to the rarefied world of France's ruling elite, with an engineering degree from a naval academy, he has also had to deal with criticism that he is underqualified for the job.
But he rejects suggestions he is a waverer on Europe or the stability of the franc.

"My adversaries have spread all sorts of rumours. That they say I am too empty-headed or too dumb, OK, but they are giving me a label (anti-Maastricht) that does not belong to me," he told Reuters in an interview last month.
In the interview Guillen said he was not against a single currency and described himself as against devaluing the franc.

"I am not in favour of devaluation," he said. "Like many industrialists, I wanted interest rates to come down a little bit faster, but that's an opinion that is an opinion of a representative of industry and that's it. I am not the only one to offer that view."

Some economists have said the choice of Guillen and Bernard to replace Boissonnat and de Maulde, who were part of a majority backing the Bank's policy of keeping its rates above those in Germany to protect the franc, could eventually tip the Bank toward easier policy to boost growth.
Sources close to the nomination process said Guillen could be expected to support this so-called dovish wing of the monetary policy council.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said after the appointments were announced, however, that they did not imply any change in policy direction.

Guillen is seen as close to Paul Marchelli, a council member who has said the Bank could cut rates by up to half a percent. Their relationship dates from the early 1970s when Marchelli began a long membership in the Parisian metallurgy union.
Guillen spent a long career with France's UIMM association of mining industries, of which he remains honorary president. He was also president of France's powerful employers' federation.
The selection process was seen as Chirac's first big chance since his 1995 election to influence monetary policy and a test of his commitment to France's decade-old "strong franc" policy.
